content:
Extreme hot weather alert in effect, yellow warning issued automatically

The Labour Department today announced a new mechanism, which continues to adopt the Observatory's Heat Index, but adds two new conditions on top of the existing warning trigger criteria, lowering the activation threshold. The first condition is that when the Observatory issues an "Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert," the authorities will automatically issue a Yellow Heat Warning, while simultaneously lowering the thresholds for the Red and Black warnings. Previously, issuing a Red Warning required the Heat Index to reach 32 or above at King's Park monitoring station or at four of the other nine monitoring stations; under the new mechanism, if the Observatory has already issued an Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert, the Red Warning will be issued as long as the index reaches 32 at King's Park or at just two of the other nine stations. According to Observatory data, the "Extreme Heat Weather" Special Alert is issued when the temperature has reached or is expected to generally reach an extreme level, that is, 35.0 degrees or above, to remind the public that the weather is extremely hot and to pay attention to their physical health.

If multiple areas reach 35 degrees with sufficient data to issue a Yellow warning, it will be directly "upgraded" to a Red warning

Another new condition of the new mechanism is that when temperatures across multiple areas of the territory reach 35 degrees or above, in addition to the further lowering of the index threshold for triggering warnings as mentioned above, any existing Heat Warning will automatically be raised by one level. Mr Hui Chak-sum gave an example: if multiple areas reach above 35 degrees and there is sufficient data to trigger a Yellow Heat Warning, it will be directly "upgraded" to a Red Warning; and when the threshold for issuing a Red Warning is met, a Black Warning will be issued directly.

The new mechanism takes effect tomorrow (the 28th). Mr Hui Chak-sum said that although this year's summer holiday is coming to an end, hot weather may continue, and it is impossible to estimate whether temperatures will rise abnormally again. The new mechanism can then be applied. Two former Observatory directors had earlier published pieces stating that the authorities had misused the Observatory's Heat Index, believing it fails to reflect the conditions endured by outdoor workers, and recommended adopting the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature used in many countries. The Labour Department stated that after the mechanism is launched, it will continuously review its operation and make ongoing improvements, such as researching whether to incorporate monitoring data such as the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature as one of the system's indicators.

Under the new mechanism, the hottest day on August 9 would have triggered a Red warning

After the Commissioner for Labour met the media, she gave a further briefing to the press. The department cited an example that on August 9, when temperatures broke records, under the new mechanism, a Red Heat Warning would have been issued. On August 8, temperatures were relatively lower, but wind speed and humidity were unfavourable, so a Black Warning might have been issued. Under the new mechanism, it is estimated that there may be four to seven days per year when a Red Warning would be issued, and one to two days when a Black Warning might be issued.

Lam Chiu-ying: Continuing to use the Hong Kong Heat Index is "a defect that needs to be addressed"

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying, who has repeatedly criticised the existing work Heat Warning mechanism, described the new arrangement as "a step forward," believing that incorporating temperature into the consideration is a down-to-earth indicator that is easy for workers to understand, and meets the expectations of frontline workers. However, he described the continued use of the Hong Kong Heat Index in the warning mechanism as "a defect that needs to be addressed," saying, "There's no reason for us to use an unscientific (mechanism) as the basis and then use other methods to correct it." He hopes the authorities will formally adopt the internationally used Wet Bulb Globe Temperature before next summer. Lam Chiu-ying also pointed out that the thresholds for issuing warnings are only the starting point; measures to cool down workers are merely guidelines, and workers have reported that they are rarely effectively implemented. He suggested listing the measures as statutory requirements.

Lee Boon-ying: The new mechanism is "a minor patch"

Another former director, Lee Boon-ying, also reiterated that the research on the Hong Kong Heat Index is not applicable to outdoor workers, and that the Labour Department's application of the Hong Kong Heat Index is "scientifically untenable." He described the new mechanism's main addition of considering temperature as "a minor patch" that fails to fully account for factors like humidity and wind, and "merely addressed the predicament of there being no higher-level work Heat Warning during extreme high temperatures," emphasising that the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature has proven effective in many countries. He said Hong Kong's hot weather season is not yet over, and the protection for outdoor workers remains insufficient; they can only look after themselves.

ICWA suggests subsidising Wet Bulb Globe Temperature equipment at worksites

The Industrial Casualties and Welfare Association (ICWA) said it is pleased to see the authorities optimising the mechanism, pointing out that the Observatory's Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert has a预警 (early warning) nature. Incorporating the special alert into consideration will, it is believed, make it easier to trigger higher-level warnings and reflect the heat stress of outdoor workers. The association also suggested the government promote and subsidise companies in setting up Wet Bulb Globe Temperature monitoring equipment at worksites, so that employers can adjust work arrangements according to on-site conditions.

ICWA also pointed out that if workers' working conditions do not improve after a warning is issued, the warning is useless. It recommended improving the existing "Guidelines on the Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work" to stipulate that high-risk outdoor work must be suspended when a Black Heat Warning is issued; for other levels, workers should be guaranteed the ability to take rest as needed without punishment from employers.

Greenpeace said this adjustment is old wine in a new bottle. By not using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and continuing to use the "Hong Kong Heat Index" that does not meet practical needs, it fails to reflect the actual heat stress of outdoor workers, and the protection is limited. Greenpeace Project Officer Yeung Kit-lai said this update is like scratching an itch through a boot. She pointed out that the conditions for issuing Red and Black work Heat Warnings still rely on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which has a relatively low weighting for "heat radiation" and is unsuitable for measuring the heat stress of outdoor workers, lacking a scientific basis. She said the Labour Department's continued use of the wrong indicator greatly compromises workers' protection.
